transcript.text: I need to flag a critical issue before we go any further. During my review of the patent ownership files this week, I confirmed that one of the patents essential to the licensed technology is jointly owned with Helix University. This means we cannot grant exclusivity — and we cannot execute this license — until Helix provides written consent. I have not circulated this finding beyond the patent file until now. This is a blocker for next Friday's target unless we secure Helix's consent immediately.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I need to add a critical data point to this discussion. I confirmed with the product business team this week that our approved commercial position is a 6.5% royalty and a $400,000 annual minimum, limited to exclusive use in hospital cardiac monitoring. The team does not approve worldwide exclusivity. I have not yet updated the negotiation summary with that benchmark, so it hasn't been reflected in our discussions with NovaBio. This is directly relevant to Thomas's point — we already had a commercial constraint on exclusivity that wasn't captured, and now we have a legal blocker on top of it.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: I need to flag a critical export-control issue. After reviewing NovaBio's technical specifications this week, I classified the licensed encryption module as subject to U.S. export controls. This means the agreement must prohibit sublicensing to embargoed jurisdictions and require export screening before each transfer. The current draft has no export-control language whatsoever, and I have not yet marked up the draft. This is a significant gap that needs to be addressed before execution — and it's directly relevant to the sublicensing provision NovaBio is requesting, which cannot be permitted without these export-control restrictions in place.

transcript.text: Thank you all for these critical findings. Let me summarize where we stand. Thomas, the Helix University joint ownership issue is a hard blocker — we cannot grant exclusivity without their written consent, and we need to initiate that request immediately if we have any chance of meeting next Friday. Nadia, your commercial position of 6.5% royalty, $400,000 annual minimum, and exclusivity limited to hospital cardiac monitoring aligns with a more constrained scope than what NovaBio has proposed. Victor, the export-control gap is significant — the current draft has no export language at all, and given NovaBio's requested sublicensing rights, we absolutely cannot proceed without prohibitions on embargoed jurisdictions and mandatory export screening. Here's my assessment: we have three open issues that must be resolved before I can approve this package. First, we need Helix University's written consent. Second, we need to renegotiate the commercial terms to reflect our approved position — 6.5% royalty, $400,000 minimum, and field-limited exclusivity to hospital cardiac monitoring rather than worldwide. Third, Victor needs to mark up the draft with export-control provisions, and sublicensing must be conditioned on compliance with those restrictions. I'd like each of you to confirm the timeline for your respective deliverables so we can assess whether next Friday is still realistic or whether we need to communicate a delay to NovaBio.

transcript.text: Thank you, Elena. On the Helix University consent issue, here's my timeline assessment. I can prepare and send the written consent request to Helix University's technology transfer office today. However, I cannot control Helix's response time — university review cycles for joint ownership consent can take anywhere from several days to several weeks depending on their internal processes. I'll flag the urgency and request expedited handling, but realistically, even if Helix responds favorably, we'll need at least 48 to 72 hours for their legal review and sign-off. That said, I want to be clear about the legal parameters: even with Helix's consent, exclusivity would still be constrained by whatever terms Helix imposes — they may limit scope, require additional royalties, or place other conditions. So there are two layers of uncertainty here: whether Helix consents at all, and on what terms. My recommendation is that we initiate the Helix request immediately, but I would advise against committing to next Friday until we have at least an indication from Helix that they're willing to consent and on what timeline. I'll report back as soon as I have a response from their office.

transcript.text: Thank you, Thomas. On the commercial side, here's my timeline assessment. I can update the negotiation summary today to reflect the approved commercial position — 6.5% royalty, $400,000 annual minimum, and exclusivity limited to hospital cardiac monitoring. I'll also prepare a redline of the commercial terms for NovaBio's review. However, I want to flag that renegotiating from 5% to 6.5%, adding an annual minimum they haven't seen, and narrowing worldwide exclusivity to a field-limited scope are all material changes that NovaBio will need time to evaluate. Combined with Thomas's point about Helix potentially imposing additional conditions on scope or royalties, we may end up with a further constrained commercial package. My recommendation is that I send the updated commercial terms to NovaBio as soon as possible so they can begin internal review in parallel with the Helix consent process. But I agree with Thomas — we should not commit to next Friday until we have both Helix's indication and NovaBio's response to the revised terms.

transcript.text: Thank you, Nadia. On the export-control side, here's my timeline assessment. I can prepare the export-control markup of the license agreement by end of day tomorrow — that includes the prohibitions on sublicensing to embargoed jurisdictions and the mandatory export screening requirements before each transfer. However, I want to flag two dependencies. First, the export-control provisions need to be coordinated with the sublicensing language that Nadia will be renegotiating with NovaBio — if the field of use or sublicensing rights change, the export screening requirements may need to be adjusted accordingly. Second, NovaBio will need to review and accept these export-control restrictions, which are entirely new terms they haven't seen. My recommendation is that I circulate the export-control markup to this group for internal review by tomorrow evening, and that it be sent to NovaBio alongside Nadia's revised commercial terms so they can review everything in one package. I agree with Thomas and Nadia — next Friday is not realistic given the Helix consent uncertainty, the commercial renegotiation, and the introduction of export-control language that NovaBio hasn't seen. We should communicate a revised timeline to NovaBio.
